answers.stem_only: Local admins can edit IAM, so IAM changes do not hold. Write one SCP that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization and attach it to the organization root, so it inherits to every current and future member account with one attachment.
SCPs never affect users or roles in the management account; the deny only binds member accounts.

An allow in an SCP must exist at every level from root to account; an account-level allow cannot add back what the OU allow list leaves out, and changing the OU SCP widens all other accounts. Move the account to a separate OU whose SCP allows the current services plus Athena.

Set up an AWS Control Tower landing zone (log archive and audit accounts, guardrails/controls) and create separate production and non-production accounts with Account Factory so future accounts get the same controls.

Create an organization and invite the existing accounts (consolidated billing gives one bill and combined volume pricing); activate the team tag as a cost allocation tag in the management (payer) account to report cost per team.
OrganizationAccountAccessRole is created automatically only in accounts created through Organizations; an invited account needs the role created by hand.

This limits what the company's own principals can do, so it is an SCP on the root that denies S3 actions when aws:ResourceOrgID is not the company's organization ID (data perimeter, trusted resources).
Register the OU with Control Tower (extend governance), enroll its existing accounts, and require new accounts to be created through Account Factory so the landing zone controls apply automatically.

Prevention, not detection: enable a Control Tower preventive control (implemented as an SCP) on the Workloads OU that denies deleting the log buckets; proactive hooks only cover CloudFormation, and detective controls only alert.
VPC sharing: share the subnets from the network account with the application accounts (or their OU) through AWS RAM; participants own their instances, the owner keeps routes and NAT gateways.

This limits who can reach the company's resources, even if a bucket policy allows it, so it is a resource control policy on the root that denies S3 access when aws:PrincipalOrgID is not the company's organization ID.

Turn on sharing with AWS Organizations from the AWS RAM console (enable-sharing-with-aws-organization, which also sets up what RAM needs), then share the Resolver rules with the organization in one resource share so new accounts get them without invitations.
